podcast.title: Child Country & Western Act (Born 1940)
podcast.body: Janice Martin was born in 1940 and began her career in early childhood as a country & western performer, pushed into this role by her dominating mother. "Janice Martin was born in 1940 and spent her early years as a child country in western act."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Secret Marriage Before RCA Signing (1955/1956)
podcast.body: A few months before signing with RCA, Janice Martin secretly eloped and married a paratrooper who was subsequently stationed in Germany. She initially kept the marriage a secret from her parents and RCA, maintaining the innocent teenage image the label desired. "A few months before she was signed to RCA, she had got married."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Debut Single Success: #35 Pop Charts, 750,000 Sales, Grand Ole Opry Performance (1956)
podcast.body: Her first single, "Will You, Will You" backed with "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll," was a hit, reaching number 35 on the pop charts and selling three-quarters of a million copies. This success led to performances on major TV shows and the Grand Ole Opry. "The first single, Will You William, backed with drugstore rock and roll, was a hit, and went to number 35 in the pop charts. It sold three quarters of a million copies, and led to performances on most of the big TV shows, as well as on the Grand Ole Opry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Signed to RCA Records at 15 (March 1956)
podcast.body: In March 1956, at just 15 years old, Janice Martin was signed to RCA Records, one of the biggest labels, by A&R man Steve Sholes, who had also signed Elvis Presley a few months prior. "in March 1956, aged just 15, Janice Martin was signed to RCA Records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: First European Tour Since 1957 (1982)
podcast.body: In 1982, Janice Martin embarked on her first European tour since 1957, performing for audiences who primarily wanted to hear her signature song, "Drugstore Rock and Roll." "So in 1982, she travelled to Europe for the first time since that 1957 tour."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Pregnancy Ended RCA Contract (1957)
podcast.body: During her 1957 European tour, her husband joined her for 30 days, and upon her return to the US, she discovered she was pregnant. RCA was furious, finding her pregnancy incompatible with her 17-year-old "nation's sweetheart" image. "When she informed RCA, they were furious. They couldn't have their 17-year-old nation's sweet heart going around being visibly pregnant."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Refused Abortion, Dropped by RCA (1957)
podcast.body: RCA attempted to persuade Janice Martin to get an abortion, which was illegal in the US at the time, to preserve her image. She refused, and as a result, the label dropped her. "She refused, and the label dropped her."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Second Marriage and Retirement from Music (1960-1973)
podcast.body: By 1960, at age 20, Janice Martin entered her second marriage. Her second husband eventually gave her an ultimatum to choose between him and her music career, leading her to quit the music industry for the next 13 years. "By 1960, aged 20, she was on to her second marriage. Her second husband toured with her for a while, but soon told her that if she wanted to stay with him, she would have to give up on the music industry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Formed Janice Martin and the Variations and Resumed Performing (After 1973)
podcast.body: After her second marriage ended, Janice Martin formed a new band, Janice Martin and the Variations, and began performing gigs again, finding renewed joy in it after years of being controlled by others. "after her second marriage ended, she put together a band, Janice Martin and the Variations, and started playing gigs again."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Third Marriage to a Fan (1977)
podcast.body: In 1977, Janice Martin entered her third marriage, this time to a man who had been a fan of hers during her initial career. This marriage lasted the rest of her life, bringing her happiness. "Her third marriage, in 1977, was to a man who had been a fan of hers during her first career, and lasted the rest of her life."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Performed with Ruth Brown, Fulfilling a Lifetime Ambition (2006)
podcast.body: In 2006, as part of her comeback, Janice Martin finally achieved a lifetime ambition by performing on stage with Ruth Brown, singing "Mama He Treat Your Daughter Mean," the song that had inspired her over 50 years earlier. "she was finally able to fulfill her lifetime ambition, and perform on stage with Ruth Brown, singing the song that changed everything for her."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Death from Cancer (September 2007)
podcast.body: Janice Martin passed away from cancer in September 2007, having outlived Elvis Presley by more than 30 years and seeing her work embraced by new generations of fans. "Janice herself died of cancer in September 2007."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: "Overtly Sexual" Performance Style & Elvis Comparison (Ages 13-16)
podcast.body: At 13 and 14, Janice Martin began dancing on stage in a manner interpreted as overtly sexual, often compared to Elvis Presley, whom she hadn't heard of and wasn't impressed by, preferring Carl Perkins. By 15 or 16, her moves were deemed "vulgar" by some, contrasting with earlier reactions when it was considered "cute." "She started performing in a manner that they interpreted as overtly sexual."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Backed by Elvis's Session Musicians (Chet Atkins, Floyd Cramer, The Jordanaires)
podcast.body: To achieve a sound similar to Elvis's records, RCA brought in key session musicians from his recordings, including Chet Atkins (who also produced her sessions), Floyd Cramer on most early recordings, and The Jordanaires providing backing vocals on some tracks. "Chet Atkins, who also produced Janice's sessions, and Floyd Kramer were both on most of Janice's early recordings, and came up with a very similar sound to the Elvis records, and on at least some of her records, the Jordanaires provided backing vocals as they did for Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Career Stalled by Misogyny
podcast.body: The narrative suggests that Janice Martin's career stalled not due to the "female Elvis" label, but due to misogyny within the music industry, which imposed limitations and expectations on her. "I think it stalled because of misogyny, plain and simple."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Day Job as Assistant Manager of a Country Club in Virginia
podcast.body: Not immediately returning to full-time music, Janice Martin held a day job as the assistant manager of a country club in Virginia, balancing this with her re-emerging music career. "She held down a day job as the assistant major of a country club in Virginia."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Disinterest in Pure Country, Preference for Honky-Tonk & R&B
podcast.body: Despite being a country singer, Janice Martin was not passionate about country music, disliking bluegrass and slow country ballads. She preferred "honky-tonk stuff" and admired Hank Williams for the "little rock" in his music. "Young Janice Martin was a country singer, pushed into the role by her dominating mother, but she wasn't massively interested in country music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Elvis Fanbase Resented "Female Elvis" Comparison
podcast.body: The teenage girl audience, who were Elvis's biggest fans, disliked and resented RCA's marketing of Janice Martin as the "female Elvis," preferring Elvis to be unique. "the teenage girl audience who were Elvis' biggest fan base started to resent the marketing, which she hadn't chosen herself, comparing her to Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Encouraged to Write Songs by Steve Sholes
podcast.body: Steve Sholes, the A&R man who signed her, not only wanted to record "Will You, Will You" as her first single but also suggested that Janice Martin try writing songs herself, leading to her first original track, "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll." "Shoals wanted to record Will You, Will You, as her first single, but had also suggested that she try writing songs herself."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: First Successful Female Rockabilly Artist
podcast.body: Janice Martin is identified as the first successful female rockabilly artist, making her a true pioneer of the genre. "Janice Martin, who as far as I can tell, was the first successful female rockabilly artist."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Guitarist from Age Four
podcast.body: She started playing the guitar at the exceptionally young age of four, holding it upright because she was too small to play it conventionally, demonstrating early musical talent. "She started playing the guitar when she was only four, holding it upright because she wasn't big enough yet to play it normally."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Incompatible Touring with RCA Country Artists
podcast.body: Because she was signed by RCA's country department and her manager was Steve Sholes, Janice Martin was placed on bills with traditional RCA country artists like Hank Snow. Her rock and roll style clashed with these acts, and the audiences were unimpressed. "Martin's rock and roll style didn't really fit on the bills, and the audiences were unimpressed."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Limited Interaction with Elvis Presley
podcast.body: Despite the marketing, Janice Martin only met Elvis Presley twice and exchanged very few words with him during those encounters. "Martin only ever met Elvis twice, and barely exchanged a couple of words with him when she did."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: MGM Screen Test
podcast.body: Janice Martin had a screen test with MGM, the film studio that had successfully signed Elvis Presley, indicating potential film career aspirations. "She even had a screen test with MGM, the film studio, the third signed Elvis up so successfully."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Marketed as "Female Elvis" by RCA
podcast.body: RCA Records actively marketed Janice Martin as their "female Elvis," seeking permission from Elvis and Colonel Parker to do so, due to her perceived similar movements and career path. "RCA decided to market her as their female Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: No Control Over Material
podcast.body: Janice Martin, like many artists on major labels at the time, had no control over the songs she was given to record, leading to her having to perform songs she disliked, such as "My Boy Elvis." "She wasn't particularly keen on the song, but she had no control over the material she was given."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: One-Time Performance with Ruth Brown
podcast.body: The 2006 performance was the only time Janice Martin and Ruth Brown ever met and performed together. "That was the first and only time Janice Martin and Ruth Brown would meet and perform together."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Parents Refused Colonel Parker's Double-Bill Offer
podcast.body: Colonel Parker, Elvis Presley's manager, sought to sign Janice Martin to a management contract and promote Elvis and Janice as a male/female double bill. However, her parents, concerned after Elvis's public collapse from overwork, rejected the offer, costing Janice the opportunity to tour with Elvis. "But her parents thought this was a bad idea."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Performing Jazz-Influenced R&B with Country Instrumentation
podcast.body: Janice Martin's unique approach involved performing jazz-influenced R&B songs by artists like Ruth Brown, LeVern Baker, and Dinah Washington with country instrumentation, a practice considered unusual even among country musicians covering R&B. "it's actually quite hard for me to imagine how one could perform Mama He Treat Your Daughter Mean in with country instrumentation. But this was what Janice Martin was doing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Pioneer of Rockabilly Music
podcast.body: Despite a lack of extensive documentation like books or films, Janice Martin's story is marked by a handful of articles in obscure fanzines and pages on unvisited websites, recognizing her as a significant pioneer of rockabilly music. "to mark the story of a true pioneer of rockabilly music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Rediscovered by European Fans & Bear Family Records (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, Janice Martin found a new fanbase, particularly in Europe, thanks to Bear Family Records, which reissued her 1950s recordings. This led to a resurgence of interest and new fans in both Europe and the USA. "But she found that she still had fans, especially in Europe."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Regular on Old Dominion Barn Dance at 11
podcast.body: By the age of 11, Janice Martin had become a regular performer on the Old Dominion Barn Dance, a notable achievement for her age in the country music scene. "by the age of 11 she was a regular on the old Dominion Barn Dance."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Sales Below RCA's Expectations
podcast.body: While Janice Martin sold records, her sales did not meet the ambitious levels RCA initially hoped for, and the label struggled to build her audience. "Janice was selling records, but not quite at the level RCA initially hoped."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Signed with Tiny Belgian Label Palette
podcast.body: After being dropped by RCA, Janice Martin turned down offers from larger labels like King and Decca Records, choosing instead to sign with the small Belgian label, Palette. "She turned down offers from King and Decker records, and instead went with the tiny Belgian label palette."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Style Change at 13 through Radio Discovery
podcast.body: At 13, Janice Martin dramatically changed her musical style after discovering Ruth Brown's "Mama He Treat Your Daughter Mean" on the radio. This led her to embrace Black R&B music, incorporating it and similar songs by LeVern Baker and Dinah Washington into her set, much to the surprise of some. "She changed her whole style with one twist of a radio dial when she was 13."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Toured Regularly Despite Hating Flying (Last Few Decades of Life)
podcast.body: For the final decades of her life, Janice Martin regularly toured, often with her son playing drums in her band, despite her aversion to flying. She felt a strong obligation to her fans to perform for them. "For the last few decades of her life, Janice Martin would regularly tour, even though she hated flying, because she felt she owed it to the fans to let them see her perform."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
